result: The study recorded single-unit activity from 23 patients with medically refractory epilepsy across 30 sessions, isolating 203 putative neurons from 68 bundles of microwires distributed across hippocampus (95 units), orbitofrontal cortex (44 units), amygdala (39 units), and anterior cingulate cortex (25 units). 47 units (23.2%) were excluded due to low baseline firing rates (<0.1 Hz).
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praised the 'incredibly rare dataset' and 'careful, high quality methodology' including task design, spike recording and sorting. One reviewer noted this is 'an important piece in the puzzle' for understanding human neurophysiology, affirming the validity of the cohort and recording methods.

result: BLA TBS modulated firing rates in 30.1% of all recorded units, significantly higher than the 15.4% responsive to no-stim trials (OR=2.37, p<0.001). Regional analysis showed units in hippocampus (OR=2.07, p=0.044), orbitofrontal cortex (OR=5.09, p=0.040), and amygdala (OR=3.33, p=0.042) were most sensitive to stimulation, while ACC showed no difference (OR=1.00, p=0.661).
evaluation: Reviewers emphasized that 'neurons in all these areas were modulated by the stimulation, except the ACC' and noted this is 'an important demonstration that low-amplitude stimulation can travel far and wide across the human brain.' The regional selectivity findings were accepted without critique.

result: Only 9.0% of units responded to both stim and no-stim conditions, despite approximately half of stim-modulated units (14.7% of all units) exhibiting changes associated with image onset. This suggests units modulated by stimulation are largely distinct from those responsive to image offset during no-stim trials.
evaluation: Reviewers praised the 'cleverly designed' experiment that 'teases apart responses due to visual stimuli (image presentation) and electrical stimulation.' They explicitly noted the authors' suggestion that 'units modulated by stimulation are largely distinct from those responsive to image offset,' accepting this interpretation.

result: Stimulation-modulated units exhibited significantly higher baseline firing rates compared to unaffected units (p<0.001), with median baseline firing rates of 1.77 Hz for modulated units in stim condition versus 1.53 Hz in no-stim condition. Location and baseline activity predicted which neurons were most susceptible to modulation.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged that 'the subpopulation that responds strongly also tends to have a higher baseline firing rate' and discussed the authors' choice of modulation index, noting it 'is more likely to be significant in neurons with higher firing rates.' The predictive relationship was accepted as demonstrated.

result: Neither stimulation amplitude (0.5 mA vs. 1.0 mA; OR=1.69, p=0.302) nor pulse frequency (33 vs. 80 Hz; 50 vs. 80 Hz) significantly altered the proportion of modulated units.
evaluation: Reviewers noted that 'low-amplitude stimulation (even when reduced to 0.5mA) can travel far and wide across the human brain,' implicitly accepting the finding that amplitude variations did not significantly affect modulation proportions. No concerns were raised about these parameter comparisons.

result: The most common epoch for firing rate modulation was during the 1s TBS delivery (25.0% of neurons), with smaller subsets modulated post-stimulation (6.4%) or both epochs (1.3%). Suppression was most common during stimulation (56.4%), while enhancement dominated post-stimulation (70.0%). Mean absolute z-scored firing rate differences were z=0.60±0.58 during and z=0.43±0.27 post-stimulation.
evaluation: Reviewers praised the 'detailed and deep investigation into the single-unit responses to intracranial stimulation' and noted the work provides 'high confidence in the validity of their findings.' The temporal dynamics and directional effects were accepted as part of the comprehensive characterization.

result: 85.3% of neurons were classified as excitatory and 14.7% as inhibitory based on waveform morphology. Stimulation appeared to affect excitatory and inhibitory neurons equally, suggesting no preferential activation of one cell type. Inhibitory neurons exhibited shorter waveform widths and greater baseline firing rates (p=0.023) than excitatory neurons.
evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about the cell type classification or the finding of equal modulation across cell types. The methodology for distinguishing excitatory and inhibitory neurons was implicitly accepted as part of the 'careful, high quality methodology' praised throughout.

result: No overall effect of memory enhancement was observed when controlling for subject-level variability (p>0.05). At the session level, 36.7% showed enhanced memory, 20.0% showed impaired memory, and 43.3% showed negligible change. No meaningful difference in proportion of modulated units was observed when grouped by behavioral outcome (all p>0.05). The impact of neuronal modulation on memory remains unclear.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the lack of clear behavioral effects without criticism, noting this 'complements the results reported in the 2018 paper' (Inman et al.). The finding that neuronal modulation did not clearly correlate with memory outcomes was treated as a valid result rather than a limitation.

result: Stimulation did not appear to alter the rhythmicity in neuronal firing, as measured by spiking autocorrelograms.
evaluation: Reviewers did not question this finding. The comprehensive analysis of stimulation effects, including what was not affected (rhythmicity), was part of the 'detailed and deep investigation' that reviewers praised.

result: TBS of the BLA primarily resulted in transient changes to firing rate coactivity within hippocampal neurons, present regardless of laterality to stimulation. Neurons exhibited highly heterogeneous responses to stimulation with respect to onset latency, duration, and direction of effect.
evaluation: Reviewers praised the work as providing 'a very useful resource to any researchers in the fields of brain stimulation and human neurophysiology' and noted it could be 'instrumental in guiding diverse research studies.' The characterization of heterogeneous responses and population dynamics was accepted as valid.

result: The median distance from stimulation contacts to white matter was 4.6 mm (range 1.5-8.0 mm). No clear association was found between proximity to white matter and stimulation-induced behavioral effects (p>0.05), despite prior research showing such proximity can influence stimulation effects.
evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about this analysis. The finding was presented as a control analysis and accepted as part of the comprehensive methodological approach that reviewers praised.

result: The study employed a visual recognition memory task with encoding (160-320 trials, 3s image presentation, ~6s ISI) and retrieval phases separated by ~24 hours. During encoding, equal numbers of stimulation (1 mA, 50 Hz TBS delivered over 1s with 50% duty cycle) and no-stimulation trials were randomly interspersed. Comprehensive spike sorting, statistical analysis, and behavioral performance metrics (d-prime) were applied.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praised the 'rigorous task design' and 'careful, high quality methodology throughout (e.g. task design, spike recording and sorting, statistical analysis).' The experimental design was described as 'cleverly designed' and provided 'high confidence in the validity of their findings.'

result: The manuscript provides extensive background on amygdala function in memory, prior BLA stimulation studies in humans and animals, TBS mechanisms, and related neurophysiological findings from the literature. These claims establish the scientific context and rationale for the current study.
evaluation: Reviewers did not question the background literature or theoretical framework. The study was described as building on prior work (specifically Inman et al., 2018) and providing 'an interesting analysis that complements the results reported in the 2018 paper.' The scientific rationale was implicitly accepted.
